rv.q: It's all that good: a sweet-soul, solid-gold, five-star blast.

The Commitments, in contrast, is thrillingly brash and raucous, and concerns a band who believe that the Irish are the "niggers of Europe" and gradually learn to belt out terrific covers of Tamla Motown, Stax and Atlantic soul classics.
Once the band is formed, the show becomes unstoppable fun, with plenty of big numbers, most of them different from the film.
But while some of its roughness is intended, some seems less carefully managed.
But the evening is much more successful as a staggered gig than as drama.
The show is exuberant, fast and funny but, in the end, more gloss than grit.
The stage version is less their own instruments and perform romantic, less interesting.

The West End is always full of shows closing, some departures are barely noticed, some deserve to close but Shaftesbury Avenue is going to be poorer when THE COMMITMENTS finishes its two year at the Palace Theatre on November 1st where it’s played more than 1,000 performances since it originally opened on October 8, 2013.
The remainder of this production is entirely forgettable and not the poster for the West End that I was expecting from this theatre.

I have mixed feelings about the new stage musical of The Commitments, which combines elements of both but somehow doesn't fly off the stage with any great theatrical pezazz in Jamie Lloyd's hard-working production.

cn.t: Critics find this energetic adaptation of Doyle's novel delivers terrific performances and belted-out soul classics, but the slight story doesn't go anywhere, resulting in a fun yet dramatically inert jukebox musical.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Palace Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
At 1,648 seats, Palace Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: Spectacularly renovated in a $100M+ project that literally raised the theater 30 feet. The restoration preserved its opulent 1913 interior while upgrading acoustics, seating comfort, and best-in-class restrooms on every level — widely considered the best facilities on Broadway.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Wheelchair, aisle transfer, and companion seating on all levels.
